utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take it that the parties have also received a set of documents provided by Mr. Krajisnik this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I don't think they've been distributed. I think that -- I think the habit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They're about to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the habit of the court staff, the registrar, and the legal officer - and I don't blame them for this at all - is not to distribute documents like that without the leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's a correct approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I make one observation in addition to this? We prepared a short bundle of documents last night. I got those to Mr. Tieger fairly late yesterday afternoon and had a chance to discuss them with him. With his agreement, they were given to Mr. Krajisnik about ten minutes ago, and Mr. Krajisnik has indicated, through the usher, to whom we're very grateful, that all bar one of the documents that we have selected are in his bundle. I hope that's a useful starting point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- so that means that the bundles are more or less of the same content apart from one document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik's bundle clearly has additional documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I suggest is the following: First of all that we check whether the documents are in evidence. When I looked at the first one this morning, just first page, I thought that it looks very familiar to me, and with the great assistance of the registrar, he is now able to give me P272, which is the document which we find as the first one in Mr. Krajisnik's bundle. So what we first should do is to see whether these documents are already in evidence. At least the first one is, that's the order to the post office in Pale to disconnect some telephone numbers, P272. So therefore, the parties are invited - and I think to the extent the registrar could assist us, he will certainly do so - to find out whether this is material already in evidence, yes or no. Second step would be for the material which is not yet in evidence, the parties try to identify what kind of documents we have in front of us. I'll leave that at this moment to the parties, and I'd like to find out whether the parties would use those documents in their -- in the examination of the witness, because if so, we don't have to specifically pay attention to that at this stage as something added by Mr. Krajisnik which was not envisaged by the parties to deal with. And then, of course, if there's any -- if there are any remaining documents, that means not yet in evidence, not intended by the parties to be covered, then of course we should pay attention to the remainder and see whether with -- whether the Chamber would invite Mr. Krajisnik to explain what these documents are and why he has drawn the -- our attention to it. But then perhaps they should be first translated -- or at least that we should consider to have them translated, perhaps on the basis of what the parties tell the Chamber is approximately the content of these documents. So without giving a full explanation but say: This is a decision by the Crisis Staff which deals with so-and-so matters. And then we can decide whether there's any need at that moment to have it -- to have a full translation and whether to address the documents, yes or no. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is happy to facilitate this process in any way we can. I should mention that the -- at least one of the Court's suggestions seems to presuppose a degree of cooperation with the Defence that has -- that doesn't precisely exist. Mr. Josse and I had contact yesterday in anticipation of what I understood to be his intended use of these documents so that he could simply indicate the documents, provide the Prosecution with some brief summary to the extent he could of the portion of the document he intended to focus on and the general substance of the document. That's as far as our discussions have gone. Therefore, if we were to move on to the next phase of the process, that is the proposed submission of documents without translations, we would be utterly at a loss and certainly not prepared to deal meaningfully with such a submission. So at this point, as indicated, we're more than willing to exercise as much flexibility as possible to assist the Defence in presenting its evidence in a reasonable manner, but the limitations should be clear, and we really don't know much about these documents and we are -- we have a responsibility to understand the document in full before we can respond to submissions or before we can be prepared to cross-examine about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there is a clear reservation as far as the OTP is concerned, but we'll then hear from you if it comes to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My position, I think, is this, Your Honour: That I was ready to continue with the examination of my client on this particular topic, based on the documents that we had selected. Bearing in mind there are additional documents here, I think the prudent course would be for me to move to another topic and come back to this, frankly, on another day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was more or less my suggestion as well, to first identify whether we have them already, and then of course I would not expect you within five minutes to say the others are vital or not vital or are going to pay attention to it and whether you would want to have them introduced without having a full -- full translation. Yet, of course, it also very much depends on what kind of documents we're dealing with. If it's a document which -- no, we'll leave it to the moment when you come back to that. I take it, Mr. Tieger, that you would at this moment not object to the proposed way of proceeding by Mr. Josse? Okay. Then let's proceed. Mr. Krajisnik, after I have reminded you, again, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I hope that everyone now has the intercept that was erroneously not in the bundle yesterday. This is the conversation between the witness and Ratko Mladic, dated the 24th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It bears the exhibit number P154, tab 33, and as I observed yesterday, as far as the Defence are aware this has never been played and I would like it to be played at this point, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]: "Yes. Hello. Yes, please. Good evening. Good evening. Mr. Krajisnik's office. Yes, please. Is General around? It's me. One moment, please. Yes. Mladic. Good evening, General. Good evening. Can you hear me? Perfectly. Can you hear me? I hear you, but be careful, there is -- between us ... I know, I know ... ... mediator. ... I understand everything. Okay. Has Minister Mandic arrived down there? He was here today, but, I don't know, it seems that he left. He will come down there. Okay. And we should ... I will find him. Okay. I have to give him some information. Okay. And now I will try and see if there is a guy with a jeep here. Okay. And please, when he arrives ... Okay. A piece of information that he conveys is related to this information. Okay. We should do that no matter what it takes. Okay. So I will try and find him now, and if I don't find him ... Okay. ... I'll send someone with a jeep to bring it to you in the morning. Okay. Because, I believe you have other things to do tomorrow, regarding this relocation. Right? No problem. If it wasn't late, you would see it now, because this is a serious piece of information that I've got. Okay. Okay. I'll try and find someone, but please, when he comes, if there are any problems, I'm quite sure you'll agree upon that. No problem. But this information has confirmed that the problem is even more serious than I thought. Okay. This is what we'll do, up there, at my place, there is ... Yes. At Milovanovic ... Yes. ... if that's not possible, if the weather's nice tomorrow morning, it should be transported with that device ... Yes, yes. That Milovanovic went by ... Yes, yes. He will come to my place, he's already on his way, just call him ... Is he on his way to your place already? No, no, but he can deliver it on his way. Of course. Milovanovic, has he been with you today? No, he wasn't here. He wasn't? And it would be good if you're in touch with him, he could come by and I could give him this for you. No, no, he's not going to be coming here... it's not a problem if it comes to me in the vehicle. Okay. Anyway, you'll receive this, this evening or tomorrow morning. No problem. Okay. Otherwise, how are you? Well, I'm fine, I'm just a little bit concerned about certain things, I think everything's fine. Everything's going to be just fine, don't be worried ... The God willing, General, right? That's right, ha, ha, ha. Ha, ha, ha. The God willing and if we do it. No, no, I know that, sometimes God can use a little help. That's right, we should help him. Thank you very much. Let me tell you, this thing went fine today, these here were fair mostly, they've been breaking my nerves the whole day, and I don't think I'll be able to manage until they ... we start in the morning, and the relocation is being carried out in the evening. Such problems I've had this evening. Because of what? Our people came here, asked me questions about the drivers that came back. Aha, don't you worry about anything ... But I tried like a real politician, and I could hardly convince them. Just tell them it's better that way, we care for lives. Yes, yes. And we'll take care about everything else. Yes, of course. Very well. Everything's going to be all right, President, don't you worry. Okay. We offered them peace, and they accepted it, I can see that they're doing it the way they should now, had they done it like this before, none of this would have happened. I know, it would sure be better than the other way. Don't you worry about anything, President ... Okay. Everything's going to be all right, don't you worry. We'll take care of those things that we have talked about, you know, dislocation. Yes, yes. And speaking about mine -- it will have to wait. Yes, yes. I will have to stay longer, I feel great here. No, no, [Realtime transcript read in error, "New York City"] I completely agree, it's all right. Here by Miljacka. You know that. Everything's all right next to Miljacka. Yes. I received information about those up there doing a great job. I'm sorry about today, the line was bad, but I think it's good over there in Lisbon. Is that right? Aha. I'll talk to you tomorrow. Okay, thanks, bye. You're welcome, bye. Say hello to everyone. Thanks a lot, bye. Bye."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What is the serious piece of information that you had before -- no, wait. I'll repeat my question, Mr. Krajisnik. What is the serious piece of information that you had for Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I don't understand. Here it says "New York" where it should say Lisbon in the text. You can take a look for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It says "Lisbon" in the English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I heard Lisbon, but on the monitor, on the screen, it came up as New York. Perhaps I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was translated as Lisbon, it appears in the writing in Lisbon, and the -- usually the transcripts are corrected during the evening hours to take out any mistakes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was -- I was at Pale, and Mr. Mladic was in Lukavica. At the time he was already commander of the Main Staff. He helped the representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army in the dislocation of barracks, moving of barracks, the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army, that is, which had still not been moved to a different location because of the blockade, the siege laid by the armed forces of the other side, that is to say the Muslim side. And at the time the Muslim side demanded that a certain quantity of weapons be given them by the Yugoslav People's Army, for them to be able to enable these members of the Yugoslav People's Army to leave the barracks. And this convoy of weapons was supposed to arrive from Belgrade via Pale going on to Sarajevo. I received information to the effect that the citizens, that is to say the population, the inhabitants, for the convoy to be able to pass through had learnt about this exchange, that they were angry, and that they could attack the column. Because I had provided this information to Mr. Mladic, they chose a different route and handed over the weapons at an UNPROFOR building in Sarajevo. They handed over the weapons to the -- the representatives, that is, of the Yugoslav People's Army and the General Staff from Belgrade. Now, I'm, telling him, I'm saying to him that Mr. Mandic will bring him that information because the government has charged some sort of coordinator in the name of the government to receive -- for Mr. Mandic to receive this information, although his role was none other than to try and collect up the necessary information so that people knew what they had done. And today, I handed over two contracts, the ones that you sought yesterday, about the relocation of barracks. You have the exercise book that I handed over to you this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, is that in the binder that you handed to everyone this morning?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, that's right. The binder, the two contracts between the Yugoslav People's Army and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is at the end. It's the first document from the end; that's how I put the binder together. One is dated the 10th of May, the other is dated the 18th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, Mr. Tieger and I had some discussions on this topic as well yesterday. Neither of us, on a cursory glance of the exhibit list, were able to identify the matter -- the documents as being there. That's not to say they aren't there. I hope I speak for both of us fairly in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It might be a document that -- since the Chamber asked whether it was in evidence, yes or no, to have this one be translated with urgency because the Chamber would like to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sladojevic has identified the two relevant documents from the bundle and has extracted them for me. Well, Your Honour, I'm anxious to deal with this at this juncture. I don't think I can put this subject off as well. Could I hand these two to Mr. Krajisnik? They're from our bundle, but it's an easier way to do it if any --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Extract them, Mr. Krajisnik, because we want to identify them, want numbers given to them, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall we put it on the ELMO so you can follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be, Your Honours, D193 and D194.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your binder this is the first document from the end. I can read the title and tell you who signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do that, please, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Contract on the departure of commands, units, and institutions of the JNA from garrisons-barracks, column, Zenica, Travnik, Konjic, and barracks and institutions in Sarajevo done on the 10th of May, 1992, in Sarajevo at the offices of the UNPROFOR. Contracting parties: 1, Presidency and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina; 2, representatives of the JNA; 3, EC monitoring team; 4, personal envoy of Lord Carrington, Mr. Doyl." And it would be important for you to see who signed at the bottom. We see two stamps here. The first is the stamp of the command of the 2nd Military District, I believe, and the second, it says: "Republic Secretariat for the National Defence, Sarajevo." That means the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the left-hand side, number 1, "for the Presidency," signed by Fikret Abdic and Stjepan Kljujic. 2, "for the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina," signed by Jerko Doko. 3, "JNA representative, Major-General Milan Akentijevic." On the right-hand side, number 4, EC monitoring team, Mr. Antonio Nanes; and number 5, personal envoy of Lord Carrington, Mr. Doyl, Kolm Doyl.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you said that you see a stamp of the 2nd Military District. Could you tell me which one of the two stamps that would be. I don't any reference to military districts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Forgive me, please. I made a mistake. It's the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo. That's the first stamp at the top. And the other one is the Republic Secretariat for National Defence, Sarajevo. So both stamps are of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you, Mr. Krajisnik, looking at the first page of this document, we see some manuscript in the left-hand margin. Do you know whose handwriting that is?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already tried to decipher it. This document was prepared and then the representatives concerned made corrections and initialled it on various pages. And we see handwritten notes on the margins; we see that on the screen. But further below in the document, there are other corrections that have been initialled. These here are just notes on the margin that I cannot decipher.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So as far as you are aware, these are parts of the original document; they're not notes that you or anyone that you know had added subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You're right. This document was found at Pale on the premises of the government, and I think the OTP didn't take the document at the time because they were not interested then. But all those documents were at the disposal of the Office of the Prosecutor. And later, going through the documents, we found this one. And I received it from my Defence team just after arriving at the Detention Unit. I didn't think originally that it would be important to us, and that changed only yesterday when the Presiding Judge sort of assigned me to find these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's look, if we may, at the one that bears the date of the 18th of May. Again, perhaps if you read the title, we might be able to work out the difference.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just give a brief explanation before I do that? The first contract we saw was the general one, and this is a contract of a more specific nature. I'm reading now: "Contract on the evacuation of commands, units, and institutions of the JNA from the Sarajevo garrison done on the 18th of May, 1992, in Sarajevo on the premises of the UNPROFOR. "Contracting parties: "1. BH Presidency and government. "2. The Yugoslav People's Army. "3: UNPROFOR." And although perhaps the entire document is important, it would be a good idea to look at the signature because there are also certain additions made, all of them initialled. "Signed: "1: For the Presidency of the Republic of BH." Two names typewritten: Fikret Abdic and Stjepan Kljujic." There is one signature I cannot decipher which means that not both of them signed this. "2: For the JNA: Colonel Branko Cadjo. "3. For the UNPROFOR: Colonel K. Hoglund." This concerns the relocation of barracks from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse and Mr. Tieger, I hardly can imagine that such a document would have been signed on behalf of UNPROFOR without an English translation, unless Mr. Hoglund was mastering the -- what we now call the B/C/S language. Could we try to find out whether a translation does exist, either made at the time or made later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll -- we will -- we will make an inquiry of such people as we have in Pale. Limited as that is, frankly, that's all we can do, but we undertake to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That effort is underway, I believe, even now and I will confirm it by e-mail immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I am producing here what I received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No need to apologise. You are kind enough to -- to find the documents. I'm addressing counsel to see whether they have any translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Going back to the intercept, it may be obvious but let me ask you anyway: Why was Mr. Mladic continually telling you not to worry during the course of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at that time a significant difference appeared between our interests, the interests of Republika Srpska, and the interests of the Yugoslav People's Army, because many people on our side failed to understand. The Yugoslav People's Army and the General Staff wanted to pull out, at all costs, both civilians and recruits and women and children from the garrisons under siege, and I personally believed it to be completely justified. They were being blackmailed, in a way, into handing over a certain amount of weapons, and our people find -- found it hard to swallow, this handover of weapons. Mr. Mladic was then commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, but at the same time he was assisting the representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army who were holding a lot of things back, even from him, because he was formerly on the other side. When we had this problem of a group of unhappy people who came bent on creating an incident, I was afraid that something might happen that would result loss of life, and I was telling him constantly that there could be a problem so that he should know. There was this meeting with us that he attended, and we talked about enabling the JNA to leave. We had to be neutral, but the least we could do is not make it harder for them, and that's why he was saying: Don't worry. We'll keep it all under control. Our role was to be bystanders. We could not be involved, and even Mladic could not get involved, and you will be able to see that from the series of conversations that he, Mladic, had with Fikret Abdic. All this was orchestrated by the JNA from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you talk about the Chamber being able to see that from the series of conversations that he, Mladic, had with Fikret Abdic, you're referring to other intercepts that you have seen, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise, but Mr. Josse and I reviewed a great number of intercepts that we received from the Office of the Prosecutor, and I am now saying that there are a lot of conversations intercepted between Mr. Fikret Abdic and Mr. Mladic other than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's move on, if we may, to the next conversation, which was three days later. This is P67, tab 32, and also P292, KID31423.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's been played twice already, Your Honour; in the course of Mr. Treanor's evidence at 1740 of the transcript, and in the course of Mr. Kljujic's evidence at 6093. But, frankly, it's of such importance that the most sensible way for me to proceed is for it to be played yet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On your list, on your cover page, it is what number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 186, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English interpreter hasn't found the text. We are very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we stop it? Could we stop it so that the English interpreter first finds the text. You've got the bundle. It's, I would say, just before half, approximately, and the cover page of that specific intercept bears as the first number 186.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have got it now. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the -- could we restart playing the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: From the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we missed some of it, so that's -- we can play it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover]: "Hello. Hello. Ratko MLADIC: Good morning. This is Mladic, the general here. Good morning. Ratko MLADIC: Is Momo there? Yes, would you hold on a sec, please. Ratko MLADIC: Please put him on. I need to speak with him pronto. All right. Immediately. Ratko MLADIC: Hello. Yes. Here, the Speaker is on his way. Hold on, please. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Ratko MLADIC: Good morning, President. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Good morning. Ratko MLADIC: How are you? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Well, okay. Did you sleep well? Ratko MLADIC: I slept well. Look, I need to tell you. We have done our part of the airport deal totally, so it should be publicised. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. Ratko MLADIC: There are some individual shots there. They opened fire, but we don't fire back. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: I'm doing that immediately this morning. Ratko MLADIC: Yes. Momo is on his way down there. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Ratko MLADIC: With these Boskovic and the others and they will be doing their job down there. Yeah. Hello? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes, I can hear you. Ratko MLADIC: I'm going further, as planned, and tomorrow I'll stop by to get new instructions. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Excellent. Ratko MLADIC: So we'll arrange for that for what we should do next. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. Ratko MLADIC: I have given Tolimir some instructions at France and elsewhere. Mm, all right. Here. I still don't have exact information on the area towards Ivan Sedlo but I hope we'll somehow manage somehow to -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We have consolidated that Trovrh a bit, so that, too, is excellent. Ratko MLADIC: That's excellent. I told Manojlo to strengthen it a little. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: You know we have a kind of situation here. Ratko MLADIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: It doesn't matter. It's just that this doesn't befit the Serb people. It can say much. Ratko MLADIC: Yes. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We are having a grand robbery of cars down in Vogosca. Ratko MLADIC: Let's not talk about that. Oh, yes, yes, you should prevent that from happening. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes, yes, yes, but let me just tell you. Ratko MLADIC: Yes? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: We have to send our military police there to arrest those people. Ratko MLADIC: No, no, military police is not to be used like that. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: It's not, is it? Ratko MLADIC: Don't, no, no. You have civilian police and let the civilian police do their job. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right. Ratko MLADIC: There's also this -- Momcilo KRAJISNIK: These people doing -- Ratko MLADIC: In Zunovnica, Momo. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes. Ratko MLADIC: In Zunovnica they steal military equipment and sell it to the Muslims. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No, if we do things like this, we will fail. Ratko MLADIC: That's right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: No way, nor can these misdeeds be done by honest people. There it's -- Ratko MLADIC: There. Civilian police should take care of this. I told the same thing to that guy in Vogosca. They told me the other day that people from the Ministry of the Interior should take control of this. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: All right, deal. Ratko MLADIC: This ministry and the judiciary should do their jobs. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: General, every people that has a general like you like this is lucky. Ratko MLADIC: Let me ask you. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Yes? Ratko MLADIC: What do you think I give a brief interview up there and call on younger pensioners to join the mobilisation? Momcilo KRAJISNIK: That would be excellent for the homeland, defensive war. Ratko MLADIC: Excellent. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There. No problem. Ratko MLADIC: Deal. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: There will be a man up there who will join you as planned. Up there at Sokolac. Ratko MLADIC: Excellent. But let him come to that centre. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: He knows. He knows where, too. You will be at the same place and he will be at Sokolac, you know. Ratko MLADIC: All right. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Deal. Ratko MLADIC: All right. Cheers. Momcilo KRAJISNIK: Bye. Ratko MLADIC: Bye."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What was your concern about the grand robbery of cars?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information came -- was coming in that this storage place for vehicles in Vogosca was exactly on the separation line where there was only a fence between two sides and those cars are being looted on a large scale. People were just driving them away. We had heard about that and it was discussed at this consultative meeting, and I thought since the army was down there I should tell him so that he can send military police to protect the location. And he tells me here that it's not the job of the military police, that the MUP should take care of that. As it happens, he was wrong, but I was just asking him to do something about it, to stop it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He pretty clearly refuses to help you out in the way you ask. How did you feel about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see here that this conversation took place in the morning. I would always get to work on time. And, as I said, Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic were at Jahorina and then they would come in a little later, as would Mr. Karadzic. So, most probably, before that he had asked to speak to Mr. Karadzic, although that's not on the tape here. And then, since I was there, he is then referring to something that we discussed at a meeting all together and where he presented these problems. So the essence of this is the following: If you recall, there was a protected witness who testified here, and when he asked him whether it was possible - he was a military man - whether it was possible for a general on the 12th of May, 1992, who was appointed general should say in his speech that he knows who his supreme commander is and that he had some sort of dilemma whether I was part of that supreme command. The clear answer was that he did know this and that we were talking here as two individuals, each having their own functions. So not all the conclusions were correct of those who attempted to represent this as being a conversation between the civilian command, myself, and a -- somebody subordinate in the army. Because here we can say that he -- see that he refers to me by name, and we would refer to each other by name in familiar terms. So Momcilo Krajisnik had no competencies there; he was fully aware of that. And from the 12th to the 27th, when the Presidency was elected, he knew who each member of the Presidency was. So the substance of this conversation was as if you would be talking to anybody occupying a responsible function and asking him to help solve a problem down there in Vogosca, because we're all on the same assignment, after all. And you'll be able to find that, or find the transcript of what the protected witness said. I asked him that. I asked him the question. And I can tell you in private session who the man was, who the witness was. And that's how it was. In the 12th of May speech, he said quite clearly: My supreme commander is such-and-such. The law on constitution is quite clear, and in 15 days' time, he couldn't have thought that I was the supreme commander, which led to an erroneous conclusion on the part of those who did not link up all these events. So that's the substance of it. It was morning. I was there always on time. I don't know where Mr. Djeric was; he lived nearby. But the others didn't live nearby in Kikinda, and Mr. Mladic is saying this -- well, from up there, so that means it wasn't in Lukavica. I don't know where this other place was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In a moment's time I'm going to put to you what a number of different Prosecution witnesses have asserted about this conversation, but just before I do that, at the very top of the second page in the English, Mr. Mladic says to you: "I'm going further, as planned, and tomorrow I will stop by to get new instructions." What did you understand by that remark and from whom was he going to get those instructions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already explained that we were all in Kikinda and, most probably, in that common room a consultative meeting was held, attended by Presidency members and myself and Mr. Mladic and the rest. I was abreast of what he was supposed to do, if I can put it that way. I believe I was. And this was probably related to the relocation of the barracks and what his role ought to be in that respect. And he, quite simply, tried to explain what he could do from his position when we have Mr. Boskovic there, a general from the JNA, and representatives -- other JNA representatives. And this can be -- best be seen later on. So, most probably, referring to the fact that I had attended that meeting, that he would come pursuant to instructions, not from me, but that he come there, he behaved in a very military fashion there and put it that way, although what he said he said as an independent, autonomous person, with full authority, because as a soldier he knew how to do this better than civilians who were now -- who now didn't know what their role was nor could they contribute to the commanding of a professional officer, to give him any instructions or orders or anything like that. When I say that, I mean the Presidency and the supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To some extent you have dealt with some of the assertions that I'm about to read out, but if there's anything you want to add, this is an opportunity, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Treanor said that this intercept was significant because it shows you dealing directly with Mr. Mladic on certain issues, particularly coordination with the Ministry of Internal --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As requested before, page reference numbers, please, if possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- the reason I didn't do that is I had given that earlier, but the answer is 1740.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you, by any chance, have a date?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. The 27th of February, 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to have to repeat that question, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Treanor said the intercept is significant because it shows you dealing directly with Mr. Mladic on certain issues, particularly coordination with the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't in contact with Mr. Mladic here; he was in contact with me. He contacted me. He called Kikinda and asked to speak to me. I assume he didn't find any of the others. He knew that I had attended this meeting, probably the one where he was talking about in the presence of Presidency members. And, quite simply, he wanted to talk to me although all this conversation is an empty conversation. He was a newly appointed general at the time. He just wanted to ring up and talk to someone, and he might have given fuller information to somebody else, or maybe not because it was an open line. But anyway, he -- Mr. Treanor is quite wrong there on that score. And you'll see that another witness overrides what he said. He was a protected witness, he was a military man, and he quite clearly said there is no general -- there is no general who does not know who his supreme commander is, from a meeting from the 12th to the 27th of May. And he attended the meeting and knew what position I held, so that's quite logical. And you will find what Mr. Mladic said at the meeting of the 12th of May where he states quite clearly who his supreme commander is. There's no dilemma on that score. It's quite another matter that Mr. Treanor, because he was harbouring a delusion, had a different thesis and tried to back it up and justify it. So this was a conversation as if I was talking to anybody, any other member of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, I am very reluctant to interfere in any way and want to see as much latitude as possible, but characterisation of witnesses as harbouring delusions -- I mean, Mr. Krajisnik is obviously blending in some argumentation with the presentation of facts. I understand that's inevitable and I haven't risen, but I just want to keep it within bounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't accept that objection at all. It's quite permissible, in my submission, for Mr. Krajisnik to comment on a Prosecution witness by saying that that witness is harbouring delusions. There's nothing wrong with that remark, it's quite proper, and the objection is most improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber's decision is that you can continue the examination and that there's no specific reason to say that this was improper. At the same time, Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber mainly listens to what it sees and might not follow strong wordings, but at the same time does not prevent you from expressing in the way you did. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, unless you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but may I be given some instructions, please? May I ask the Court something for guidance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, you're a witness, so it seems that you think that Mr. Treanor was wrong. There's no problem in telling us that Mr. Treanor was wrong and that you even strongly oppose against his views, so there's no problem. The Chamber will look at what Mr. Treanor said and the reasons why you disagree perhaps more than the language you use in order to explain that to us. Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, might I just be allowed to be given clear-cut guidelines by you so that I can tell you and you can tell me whether I'm right in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a remark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am concerned about this because later on, probably today and certainly in the course of the next few days, I'm going to go through with Mr. Krajisnik the evidence in outline of a number of witnesses and he may well make some rather robust remarks about those witnesses' veracity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try to explain. Let me give you an example, Mr. Krajisnik, if that would guide you. If you really disagree with what someone said and you find that not only wrong but very wrong, you could explain to us that it's totally wrong what he said and totally unacceptable. You, of course, could also say that he's an idiot. Well, the one might come close to the other. If you explain to us why he's wrong, what his misinterpretations were, then whether you add to it that it was an idiot or not an idiot does not perhaps assist the Chamber very much. It's, rather, the explanation you give that we are able to follow. And if you add to that that someone, for example - I'm just giving an example - would be an idiot, then of course the Chamber is aware that what your emotions are when hearing that testimony or how you understand that testimony to be. We're not keeping you off from doing it; at the same time, you should be aware of what you are expressing at that time. Of course the Chamber is primarily interested to know why you consider it totally wrong, what the witness said, and if you find it important for us to express some of the emotions it brings to you by using such kind of language, we'll not stop you from doing it, but please be aware for yourself what you're conveying to the Chamber. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I need to be given some instructions. I seem to be making mistakes, but I'm -- I don't feel that I'm making mistakes. So can I just be allowed to explain why I said what I said? I understand what you're telling me, but I would like to add something, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We feel no need that you add anything. It's not held against you that you use these words, otherwise we would have stopped you, but I hope that my guidance was sufficient. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I may say, Mr. Krajisnik, I think what the learned Judge said is clear, and just bear in mind what he said.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would like to move on to Mr. Kljujic's assessment of the intercept that we've just heard. He said that it took place in the context of the subordination of the political and military leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, that it's indicative of your authority through informal channels, and that you knew a lot about the situation on the ground. That is at page 6093 on the 27th of September, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kljujic was not well-versed in this matter and explained it quite erroneously. Now, what I want to explain now is something that would probably be outside my domain, so I'm going to be handicapped on that score. I don't know whether I can say what I want, that's why I wanted to clear this up a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Please say what you want, exactly what you want. That's what the learned Judge has just said.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kljujic and all the witnesses that you enumerated, witnesses who -- some were expert witnesses, some were witnesses who had a certain amount of authority. Anyway, I wanted to indicate certain evidence and logics in order to substantiate my own statement because we don't have an expert witness that would be presented as a counterpart to Mr. Treanor and be able to provide an explanation. That's why I asked for a little leeway; thank you for your understanding. Because it is my aim to help you, to assist the Court, to have as many arguments as possible, because you can't have just one brain, there's no one brain that can pull all this information together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just give your explanation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljujic signed -- well, I said that Mr. Kljujic was not right and that he wasn't informed about the matter, and I can guarantee here and now that he signed the contract on the relocation of the barracks, which means he said something without having the necessary knowledge and said that I was the commander. He doesn't know that the Assembly meeting took place, he doesn't know who the commander was, Mr. Mladic; he knows nothing but he wants to say something anyway. He is quite incompetent in the matter. I don't want to say anything bad about any man; that wouldn't be proper. But the truth is that he didn't have the knowledge as to who the supreme commander was and who was subordinate or superior to whom. And I can state quite definitely that the text was as I had explained it to you. Had I been his commander, he wouldn't have addressed me as "Momo." He didn't say "Supreme Commander." And when he said "President," when he referred to me as "President" or "Speaker," it would be like me saying to him "General." It's according a title out of decency and proper conduct, if you like. Manners.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, at page 16220 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have the date, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- when asked about this intercept, said that it would seem to be that a senior member of the Bosnian Serb leadership was able to speak to Ratko Mladic and give him instructions, and that would seem to show that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there we go. It's the same example. Let me explain. I'll explain why Mr. Brown is not correct on that score. It's not right. Mr. Brown does not know which premises I was on. He doesn't know that Karadzic was late. He doesn't know that Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic were at Mount Jahorina. He doesn't know that an Assembly was held 15 days prior to that. He doesn't know that we enacted a law on defence, because Mr. Mladic proposed the law and he knows who the supreme commander is. He does not know that Mr. Mladic at that time worked to help with the relocation of the barracks. He knows none of these facts, and he doesn't even know what this "Momo" means and what the reference to "President" means or "Speaker" means, whereas he's trying back up his point of view, his thesis. Now, I would have asked him these questions had I been in a position to do so, but I wasn't. And of course my Defence counsel weren't able to ask him that because we hadn't prepared for those kinds of questions and answers. But as I say, his conclusion is quite erroneous. It was by some inertia that he was moved to make these erroneous conclusions. He was just swayed that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'd like to make one brief comment. That is the following: Mr. Krajisnik, when you're still sitting there, I think this Chamber has never denied you any request to consult with counsel for additional questions to be put to a witness. I leave it to that for the time being. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to move away from the intercepts for a little while. I'm going to begin the witness exercise. Some may think this a strange choice, but I'm going to begin with John Wilson and I'm going to begin with him because it has some bearing on the military matters to which you have just been referring to. He said of you at page 13064 that you were central to the negotiations regarding the airport; that you were quite clearly, by the group dynamics, involved; clearly consulted; involved in discussions to decide when there were breaks; and quite central to the final agreement that the airport could be handed over to the UN. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall a single meeting which I attended when there was a discussion about an airport. Not a single meeting of that kind. I don't remember ever having seen Mr. Wilson until I was sitting here in court, which does not exclude that I happened to be at a meeting when he was with one of the representatives of the Serb side and put in charge of the matter of the airport. It was Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic who were in charge of the airport. And on behalf of the government, it was Mr. Mandic and I don't know who else, to assist. And on the 27th, or perhaps the 28th of June, the airport was handed over. That was Vidovdan, St. Vitus Day, and on that day I was at Ilijas and it was Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic who were at the airport, because that was when the airport was handed over. Before that, and as far as I remember, at that time the president of France, Mr. Mitterand, was visiting, so that gives you a rough idea of the time and events. They discussed the conditions, and for a time there was Mr. Mladic, for a brief period, and Mr. Ostojic included in the negotiations, but I was never there myself, not one single time. So I don't know how come Mr. Wilson mentioned me as having attended a meeting and someone having consulted me. I even attended meetings where resolute demands were made of Mr. Koljevic to explain under what conditions and why the airport was handed over in the first place, and I know that there was a government session which I did not attend where the members asked to be informed about how this handing over of the airport came about. So what Mr. Wilson said I completely deny because I don't ever remember ever having seen the man, and whether I had any meetings with him in some other circumstances, I really don't know. But this is possibly why he arrived at that erroneous conclusion. If he had a meeting in Lukavica, for instance, and if I happened to be in Lukavica in some other office on some other business while he was having talks there with someone, he might have thought that they were stepping outside to consult me. But the fact of the matter is as I have explained it to you, connected to the airport. There are telephone conversations, there are many arguments which testify to who the participants in the airport negotiations was. You have the SRNA news agency reports as to who signed Mr. McKenzie and the others, but the name Momcilo Krajisnik is nowhere mentioned because it was just not my job to do things like that. So I don't exclude the possibility of my having been perhaps at Lukavica and he might have been in some other office and thought that someone was leaving the office to consult me, but that's just not true. I had nothing to do with the whole airport issue at all. The airport was handed over in two stages; one for humanitarian purposes and the second time permanently to the UN forces and their use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, my apologies for not listening better when you said, "I am moving away from the intercepts." I have two very small informative questions about the last intercept played. Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Mladic is speaking about the area towards Ivan Sedlo. I have got no idea where that is. Could you tell me where it is. Not in detail, but is it in Sarajevo area or is it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's as you go from Mount Igman towards Mostar. That is to say south of Sarajevo, down there in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At a distance of approximately, from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's maybe as much as a hundred kilometres away. It's not close, anyway. I don't know what he was actually talking about there. Probably he had given out some information or received some information the day before and then continued along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said: We have consolidated at Trovrh a bit. I have got no idea what that is. Is that a place, is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a repeater station at Zepa where a unit was destroyed. The Muslim forces had taken control of it and then we were informed that the situation had been put right, although he probably knew that already. I do apologise. Just a moment, please. There refers more to the climate and general mood at Pale that prevailed around this Trovrh because it was a forerunner to what was to happen later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Repeater station, that's radio communication used for public broadcasting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, both radio and television repeater stations, or station. It wasn't operative; it was just a point that had been damaged. And it's referred to as Trovrh because it is the dominant elevation, but there was a repeater station there anyway and something was damaged, I can't remember exactly what. But it is this Trovrh where you have the relay station. Whether it was operational or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say the Muslim forces had taken control of it, but the situation had been put right. Does that mean that Serb forces had re-taken control or -- or that you, by any other means, by any diversion, got those radio signals where they would have to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This has to be completely -- this was completely separate from the radio signal. I'll tell you what our interest in this was. Some people had come and reported that there were some civilians besieged at some sort of platform encircled by the Muslims and nobody knew anything about their fate. And it was probably about those people who were the crew of this retransmitter. I must have been talking about them. They were encircled by the Muslims, and I don't know how this was resolved. But the whole problem was about those people, who could easily get killed, and some did get killed, as far as I know. I didn't mean that some military action had been taken. I was just talking about dealing with the problem, saving those people. It must have been an operation that had nothing to do with Mladic because obviously he didn't know anything about it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, needless to say that you raised the issue during a telephone conversation with Mr. Mladic, Mr. Krajisnik. Please proceed, Mr. Krajisnik. Yes, Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, I just wanted to know how you were informed. How were you informed about what was going on at a hundred kilometres or 150 kilometres from where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Trovrh, which means three-point summit, is in the Romanija area, Mount Romanija. It is connected territorially with Pale. How I received that report, I don't know, I can't remember anymore. Maybe there was a telephone line or maybe somebody had come to tell us. In any case, all the news, good and bad, spreads very fast. But it happened in that area that wasn't severed from us, it was accessible. You could travel on the ground as well. There was a duty officer there in Kikinda, and he must have received this report during the night. And there was also the reports and information sent that was operating. In any case, I don't remember how, but I received this report that morning when I came to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I'll finish General Wilson off before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then expectation should come through, so we have a break now. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, there's been some discussion in the break amongst the Defence team about the learned Judge, Judge Hanoteau's question, and in particular where Trovrh is. If I give you a clean map of Bosnia, could you mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, the Madam Usher, very helpfully, suggests on the ELMO. Could Mr. Krajisnik be provided with the relevant-coloured marker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is the black one. And could we zoom in a bit so that we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trovrh should be somewhere on the boundary between Pale and Gorazde, if I remember correctly. It should be written -- the name should be written somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We have not been able to locate it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it should be somewhere there, but I really can't make out what this says. It should be here where I'm pointing, but I'm not sure because I can't make it out. I think that it's here on this stretch, but I'm not sure because I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we see, perhaps, on that map is an elevation, I think it is at so many and then 74 metres where the text comes close to what we find in the -- okay. Well, you have situated that. Mr. Krajisnik, then perhaps, since we have the map in front of us, then Ivan Sedlo as well, please, if you could find that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivan Sedlo should be somewhere between Sarajevo and Mount Jablanica. It could be here. Let me just have a look. It's near Konjic, which means it could be a bit further below. Right here. That's where Ivan Sedlo is, somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then for the record, the marking south-east of Sarajevo is Trovrh, and then the marking -- overmarking further to the west is Ivan Sedlo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does Your Honour want that exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D195, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I would like to have a closer look at the exhibit. Could it be put from the ELMO, and could it be given to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more reservation. I cannot be accurate because I cannot identify it exactly, but it should be somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Parties are invited to verify the correctness, and if there's any serious doubt about it, to report to the Chamber what in their, preferably common, view is the location of these two places. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm returning to the evidence of Mr. Wilson. He made some -- what are very general observations about an important aspect of this case - some would say to put it mildly - and that is the relationship between the political leaders of the Bosnian Serbs and General Mladic. He was asked about this, of course, in the context of the airport negotiations, and he said: "It seemed to be a very comfortable relationship. They were relaxed in each other's company. There was a free exchange of information. General Mladic was not afraid to disagree with members of the political leadership, but in the end he claimed that he was subordinate to the political leadership and followed their direction." This was at page 13066.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Wilson gave what was a true picture at the time, because the handover of the airport was within the jurisdiction of the civilian authorities, and although Mr. Mladic as a soldier was involved in a way, it was within the jurisdiction of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic and some other personalities. I know there were a lot of participants who were members of various commissions that were involved in the handover and take-over of the airport, but I personally wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One final aspect of Mr. Wilson's evidence. He described meeting you at the International Peace Conference for the former Yugoslavia in Geneva at the end of 1992/the beginning of 1993. He was asked about your role as he observed it, and he said: "Mr. Krajisnik did not have a lot to say. I assume this is because he didn't speak English, but certainly he was very carefully consulted by Mr. Karadzic. He sat at a central part of the table, and he seemed to be a very important member of the delegation." This was at page 13077.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't rule out the possibility that Mr. Wilson attended that meeting because the representatives of military authorities -- military representatives were frequently part of the teams from the international community and the European Community. On our side it was usually Mr. Mladic and Mr. Tolimir who were military representatives. I remember the name "Wilson," but the Wilson I remember was a general from England. I met with him several times, but it was at a later stage. I simply couldn't place this man as if I had never seen him before. I never discussed the airport with him, and he doesn't look to me like the person -- like the Wilson I knew. The Wilson I knew was not in Geneva; he was close to the top man on the ground. I think it was a Belgian general. I can't remember his name. Excuse me, as for my role, if I understood your question correctly: Our delegation, Karadzic, Koljevic, Krajisnik, and, most frequently, Buha, always sat at the main table, and the other three parties sat opposite us; international representatives, Muslim, and Croat representatives. We were the negotiators, we were the negotiating team. And those who assisted - if that's what he means - usually sat behind us or sometimes didn't even attend. As for my role, it is true that Mr. Karadzic chaired the talks as head of delegation, but we simply talked about all the issues. He consulted others, not only me. He always wanted to consult all the other members of the delegation because he was one to say more people know more, and he was always looking for a shared opinion rather than imposing his own. When necessary, he consulted us, and at other times he would simply table his ideas and proposals for discussion. I didn't speak mainly because I didn't speak English, and if that was the procedure, if that was in order, I was able to say something to Mr. Karadzic. The interpreter usually sat next to me, and the conversation was in English and I had no time or opportunity to say much. But most importantly, I am not denying that I took an active part in those talks aimed at establishing peace, but the way that he interprets that and his conclusion that I had a strong influence is a wrong impression because we worked as a team, and we were absolutely committed to finding the best solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm now going to move on to a completely different topic and a very different witness, and I'm going to ask you about the evidence of Milorad Davidovic. Before I do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, before you continue, I noted that in relation to these meetings questions were put to Mr. Wilson as far as confronting the delegation with accusations of ethnic cleansing were concerned. You have not dealt with that. May I take it then that at least you do not expect any further information from this witness on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't follow Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, some questions were put as to what was put to the other delegation also in terms of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand that bit. It's the very last remark of Your Honour. You do not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's those words I don't follow, "any further information."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As it stands now, the witness has given his comment on the influence he would have. He has not given any -- no questions were put to him in relation to whether in this respect the testimony of Mr. Wilson is contested. And to be quite honest, I don't remember exactly what was asked in cross-examination, but of course it is a matter which is not without importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, may I make two remarks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: First of all, I'm working from some potted notes, and for what it's worth - and I'm not criticising the person who has prepared these for me - that isn't within the notes that I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Secondly, what I am very aware of is, of course, time. We are certainly at some point going to deal with Mr. Krajisnik's knowledge of events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to -- perhaps you can understand this as -- but you seem to be aware of that, that knowledge. And this is of course, since we specifically deal with this portion of the evidence, that knowledge is -- is part of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I make this observation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are, of course, certain upsides in doing things in the way that I am now doing it, namely dealing with specific witnesses. There is also a downside. The downside is it all becomes jumbled chronologically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we are aware of the advantages and disadvantages, and to some extent, as best we can, we are trying to weld these two completely different approaches to Mr. Krajisnik's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, as I've already said, to the evidence of Mr. Davidovic, but before I do that, I don't think, to the best of my recollection - and I'll be corrected if I'm wrong - you have yet been asked about your knowledge of events in Bijeljina in early April, 1992, and in particular, Mrs. Plavsic's visit there and her dealings with Arkan. So perhaps you could begin by telling the Trial Chamber what you know of those events.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events in Bijeljina came under the competence of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the delegation at one point in time was a BH government delegation visiting Bijeljina, and on another occasion it was a delegation of the Presidency, which we heard about here, which included Mrs. Plavsic. Now, as far as what Mrs. Plavsic said and recounted is quite a different picture. She said it publicly at a press conference, and it was - how shall I put this? - much more positive, without placing the blame on anyone, compared to the picture depicted by the Presidency and put out publicly as to why it sent its delegation, its own delegation. I did not consider it to be in my remit to deal with this, nor did I do so, but I knew about the problem, I knew about the issue. What I did do, however, is this: I called a deputy to come to Bijeljina when these things were going on. I was in the offices or cabinet of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this man's name was Mr. Novakovic, and I asked him what was going on. And he said: I can't tell you over the phone, and somebody snatched the receiver away from him, and I heard the voice of a man who says: While you're sitting down over there, we're doing your work for you. And who was that? That was Mr. Mauzer. So I didn't learn know anything more than that nor did I know anything more than that. Afterwards, as some sort of power and authority, he interrupted the telephone conversation, put down the receiver, and I didn't make an effort to learn anything more about that. But all the knowledge and all the actions were very far from being within my competence, nor did I deal with matters of that kind because I considered that legitimate legal organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina existed on the one side and the Yugoslav People's Army on the other, who were supposed to see to that unfortunate event, as we referred to it, but then we later on saw that this was a much more serious problem, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So what did you learn of Mrs. Plavsic's visit there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't learn anything about it from her because she was in the Presidency and I was in the Assembly, but I heard, in listening to her press conference, I heard her say that it was not correct and that even Mr. Abdic said that it was -- that what Mr. Izetbegovic dramatically -- how he dramatically presented the situation just wasn't correct. So, quite simply, they shut themselves up in the Presidency, and then another delegation went to Brod and then Kupres, and they would send out delegations in this way to try and deal with the situation which was a pre-war situation, in fact. And I can tell you of what story I heard later on as to what happened in Bijeljina, but that is second-hand, hearsay information. But this was, anyway, several years later and I think it was presented here and that story was told here by someone, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic alleges that he was involved in a number of conversations in Bosnia and Belgrade, where both you and Mr. Karadzic were present, and that Frenki and Arkan attended and you spoke to them. More specifically, he said that one of these took place in Bosanska Villa. He went on and said: "Whilst we were sitting down, there was a kind of preparation for us in -- and the federal SUP and the units of the state security service that Frenki was in charge of would be sending down, and Arkan came in with his people. And his people were there as well in the course of those talks and we all talked together and there was a distribution of tasks being decided, who was supposed to do what." And clarification was sought on the issue from the learned Judge, Judge Orie. And he, Mr. Davidovic, said both you and - as he called him - President Karadzic were there. This is at approximately page 14256. What do you say about all that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in my life have I seen Mr. Davidovic. As far as I'm concerned, he is somebody I do not know, and it is quite incorrect that I ever sat down at a table in that way. I didn't even know Mr. Arkan before. In 1995, I happened to come upon him by chance in Bijeljina for three minutes. I didn't know what the man looked like before that. So what Mr. Davidovic is saying - and I followed his testimony closely - he corrected his impressions of the meeting later on. It would appear that I and Karadzic were in the hallway, whereas they were sitting down at a table and preparing the matter. You can check that up, but I remember him saying that afterwards. Now, whether somebody was sitting at a table while we were in the same villa, perhaps, at that time, I cannot exclude that. I can't rule that out. But it is quite erroneous, absolutely incorrect, that I was sitting down at a negotiating table with him. Neither did I sit with Arkan or Stanisic or the other Stanisic or Frenki or anybody else, nor did I attend that meeting, nor did I know about this action he was to launch. You can find that portion, and you'll see that later on he corrected himself and said that we were in the hallway, corridor, while they were sitting at a table somewhere. I remember that well. I remember him correcting himself on that score. But as I say, I don't remember him at all. I didn't utter a single word to him. We never spoke at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He said a couple of pages earlier in his evidence -- he was asked: "What was your source of information that Mr. Karadzic knew about Arkan?" And he said: "Well, Mico Stanisic informed me of that, and a number of occasions I was in Sarajevo and Pale and Vrace when contact was established and the people I was with spoke about this." Can you comment on Mico Stanisic's relationship and knowledge of Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what their relationship was, but I do know about the relationship between Karadzic and Stanisic, and I can assert that it was normal and that Mr. Stanisic could talk to Karadzic. As for Arkan, I really don't know whether he knew him, what their relationship might have been, if at all, or anything like that. I do believe that he made a statement about that, we can check it out. He was here, he can probably confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, who are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about Stanisic. Stanisic was here in the Detention Unit, and I assume he made a statement, but that can be checked, too, whereas I don't know myself. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You mean before he was given provisional release?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I assume. He was in another area of the unit. I assume he had to make a statement and was then released; I don't know that for a fact, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In his witness statement, which is P764, Mr. Davidovic said that: "Mico Stanisic, who at this time was stationed in Bijeljina, came to see me whilst I was in Bijeljina and said that he had a request from the SDS leadership that something be done about the gang that was out of control and running around Zvornik. Mico Stanisic told me that Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik had told him that they were sick and tired of the problems with Zvornik." What do you say about that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there was someone -- or rather, that there was an ugly situation going on in Zvornik. And at the consultative meetings that we had, Mr. Stanisic was very often criticised and said -- and told that this had to be settled because people couldn't act arbitrarily and do what they liked over there. So that's as far as my knowledge goes. Your Honours, you have the minutes from a government meeting where the government is giving Mr. Stanisic an assignment to go to Bijeljina and see the matter through, and he went after that. Now, I have read those minutes, the record. So the government made it incumbent upon him, after the consultations held, to go there. Now, whether he was there with Mr. Davidovic or not, I really don't know, I can't say. But judging by all he indicators, it does seem that he did have some sort of contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the same witness statement, he said that: "Mico Stanisic had advised that these paramilitaries were not under the control of the army, that they had allegedly arrived in Bijeljina, and were still under the control of Mauzer and Arkan. Colonel Ilic told me that these paramilitaries apparently had the full support of the SDS in Bijeljina, that they were exclusively SDS members, and they also had the support of Karadzic and Krajisnik." What do you say about that assertion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the situation and any support from Momcilo Krajisnik, there can be -- there was absolutely none of that. That's completely incorrect. I didn't know at the time about his conflict with the leadership of the SDS - and I'm thinking of Mr. Davidovic. He wasn't somebody that I thought about. And Mr. Mauzer, that is true, was -- there was a special unit from Bijeljina. And people from Bijeljina saw them as being an elite unit. That's true, but not the SDS but all the citizens from Bijeljina. At that time when this was going on, what the relationship was with Arkan and what role and links Arkan had with Mauzer, I really don't know. It was something that was completely alien to me. But Mauzer was not negatively assessed by the leadership, as far as I knew, the leadership from Bijeljina. Not the SDS but anybody who meant anything in Bijeljina, prominent people in Bijeljina. As far as Mr. Davidovic is concerned and their links and Mr. Arkan and their links and relationships, that's something I know nothing about. I had absolutely no need to meddle in any of this, nor did I lend my support to Mr. Mauzer, nor did I, at the back of my mind, ever think that I should lend my support to somebody, nor was that necessary. He had support because they were proud of these Panthers of his. Later on all this changed, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek one clarification, Mr. Josse. You said, Mr. Krajisnik: "But Mauzer was not negatively assessed by the leadership, as far as I knew, the leadership from Bijeljina, not the SDS." Could you tell us: Who were the non-SDS members, if any, in the Bijeljina leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I said not only the leadership but the whole people from Bijeljina. It was the generally accepted view. Now, who was in the leadership there I cannot remember. But, for example, to quote an example, people in power in the SDS, if that's what you're interested in, but I meant that it was the general opinion in Bijeljina, the prevailing opinion in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what it says first where you said: "And people from Bijeljina saw them as being an elite unit, that's true, but not the SDS but all the citizens from Bijeljina," which I understood to be not SDS, people excluded from that. However, a few lines later it says: "Mauzer was not negatively assessed by the leadership, the leadership from Bijeljina."
