And then it reads in our transcript, "not the SDS," but I do understand that in that respect you also said the whole of the leadership, the SDS not excluded from them. Is that a correct understanding? That would be in line with your earlier -- with the earlier part of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The leadership -- who was in the leadership? Probably mostly members of the SDS, but not because they were members of the SDS, not by that virtue, but because they were leaders in Bijeljina. So it was from those positions that they lent their support, and it was an elite unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did they ever express that -- do you have any knowledge of them expressing that they said: Once we assess Mr. Mauzer in such-and-such a way, this is not a party view, but this is just our view as -- I don't know exactly what leadership would then mean, but from other positions -- is that distinction which you make now, was that ever, as far as you know, expressed by those who made assessments of Mr. Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me help you out here, Mr. President. Mr. Mauzer, very soon, took control of the police station. He did something bypassing the leadership, so their inclinations towards him changed. Now, which leadership? The president, the Executive Board, the president of the Assembly, that's what I mean, if I can term that to be the leadership. So I don't exclude the representatives of the SDS either, the key people. But the key people in Bijeljina who meant something is what I mean when I say when I think about the general concept of leadership. Perhaps they were members of the TO or commanders. So I'm speaking in general terms, not specifically. I know that there were none of these prominent personages who had anything negative to say about him at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you -- when you're talking about these prominent personages, could you give any example of someone who was not an SDS member who expressed himself in such a way that it could not be understood to be a negative expression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I cannot quote an example here and now. I can't quote the example of a statement by such-and-such. All I know is the prevailing opinion at that time and the impression one gained, or perhaps somebody had conveyed what the situation was like. But if I were to be concrete and say it was the president of the Executive Board or the Assembly who said this, then that would be guesswork on my part. But the general impression I gained - and I think it was the right impression - that all the people over there, both your ordinary citizen and some functionaries as well, considered him to be the commander of the elite unit of Bijeljina and they were proud of him. So that was the general impression that I gained and I'm almost certain that that was the prevailing opinion at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to find out to what extent that impression or that assessment was shared by all -- by all ethnicities in Bijeljina. That was the reason for my questions. If you could add anything -- yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said I'd tell the truth. I contacted with the Serbs, so there's no question of me contacting the Muslims, for example. I would probably have received a different answer. I'm talking about the leadership with whom I had some sort of contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that clarifies the matter. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Moving on to a different aspect of Mr. Davidovic's evidence, and this relates to his suggestion that he saw a document signed by yourself that authorised the resettlement of people in a humane way. He said that he was shown this document by a man called Djurkovic from Bijeljina, and that Djurkovic said that he shouldn't be obstructed in his work. And it said: "The president of the Assembly" in the heading of the document, and your signature was upon it. Later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That, Your Honour, was at 14318.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In cross-examination at 15282, he was asked about the document. He said: "In the upper left-hand corner it said 'president of the Assembly.' There was a signature. I can state with certainty that it was him." And then he describes why he wasn't able to get hold of the document at the time. Any truth in this allegation, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's not even one-thousandth of a part of the truth there. Let me repeat: I never issued a document like that, a document to Mr. Vojkan Djurkovic - there's a mistake in the name here - nor did I have any contacts with him. And let me remind the Trial Chamber here, that when I asked Mr. Davidovic a question, wanting to show him a document which resembled what he might have seen at the time -- well, I wasn't successful in that, I didn't succeed in doing that. So my answer is: I had absolutely nothing whatsoever to do with that. And I think that it was not that he was not telling the truth, but he was under an illusion, although some thing in certain cases he was not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I will come later on in my questioning to his motivation for saying these things. But dealing with this in a bit more detail, he said -- this is Mr. Davidovic, that he spoke to Dragoljub Micic and said: "I can't confront that. I'm familiar with that very same document." And he, Dragoljub Micic, apparently had asked you about it and you told Mr. Micic not to meddle in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I see my learned friend saying it's Mr. Mandic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, no, no. Could I just have a page reference, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think this is at 14318 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the transcript originally it said Mico Mandic. That was later corrected to Dragoljub Micic. This definitely involves -- the allegation involved your dealings with Dragoljub Micic; there's no doubt about that. What do you say about that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is invented, something that's been invented. And when Mr. Davidovic testified, our investigators contacted Mr. Micic, and he made a statement which was confirmed and which you have in which he explains that he never talked about this to Mr. Davidovic. So I'd like to have you show the statement or perhaps call -- no, you can't call him because he's just suffered a heart attack. But there is a statement that was certified by the Court where he denies those allegations. We also have Mr. Djurkovic's statement certified in the same way. You have all those documents and you can see for yourselves. You have Mr. Momcilo Micic's statement when he replaced him, what he said about Vojkan Djurkovic, but he never contacted Mr. Davidovic. You have those statements in your possession, and they were certified by the Court. So -- well, he even said that Micic presented this before the Assembly. Now, you have records from all the Assembly meetings. That issue was never on the agenda. He heard about that somewhere and then just recounted it further. And as I say, I'm sure you'll be showing the Trial Chamber that document in due course, the one I wanted to show them, so that they could see what this was about. A document does exist but not Momcilo Krajisnik's document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some specific questions and try to give a specific answer. Who was Dragoljub Micic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragoljub Micic was a deputy from Bijeljina. He was together with me in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serb Assembly as well, and he is Momcilo Micic's brother, Momcilo Micic being the man who testified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this implicates a matter that was raised yesterday - I believe it was yesterday - in connection with the introduction of -- it was a discussion about statements or documents and the distinction between the two, the 92 bis implications, and so on. We discussed that in reference to the submission of statements that hadn't met the requirements of 92 bis. The Court is aware of our objection, and that issue was tabled for consideration by the Defence, presumably. In light of our position, that should not be circumvented by the -- by eliciting testimony about those statements in lieu of simply submitting them; it's the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it seems that it would not be hearsay evidence but see-say evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, two observations: The first is that I didn't invite that answer to the question, and Mr. Tieger didn't suggest that I did. Indeed, yesterday he was at pains to point out that that wasn't the purpose behind my question. But secondly, it's really in relation to Your Honour's observation, and that's this: There is certainly an argument -- it's quite a big topic and perhaps now's not the time to argue it, so to speak. But there is an argument that it is hearsay, like any other bit of hearsay. This Chamber allows witnesses to say what they've read in a book, what they've heard from other people. What, I ask rhetorically, is he material difference between that and a witness in this case, who happens to be the accused, who says: I've read a witness statement, and the witness statement says X, Y, and Z. But I'm not encouraging the Chamber to hear argument on that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first of all, there are no other specific rules on telling from what you read in a book, where there are specific rules on the admission of statements. I mean, Rule 92 bis, of course, gives a full set of -- I would say a set of guarantees, what could be in such a statement to be admitted, what would not be -- whether that witness would have been warned that giving a false statement would be contempt, et cetera. I mean, there's a whole set of rules about that; there's no set of rules about what one read in a book. But I -- until now, I think our present witness said that this could be confirmed by reading statements, et cetera, and we have not heard any details about it. I also noted that you said that you were not eliciting this kind of evidence from the witness at this moment. So for the time being, if that would not change, then it's a mere statement that in another -- the mere testimony that in another statement it is confirmed or it is not confirmed without giving any opportunity as it stands now, since that statement is not available for us to verify that. That, of course, would -- might have some consequences, since there are clear ways of introducing written statements. But as it stands, for now we just proceed. And I well understood that it is -- this is not the moment that you would like to fundamentally raise the issue, which I would expect you to do if you would go any further on this route. Please proceed, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik - I hope the learned Judge will permit me to say this to you - it is apparent and obvious to everyone in this courtroom that this is a subject that you feel strongly about. For my part, by all means, give a robust answer to the question. But it's really your views and your knowledge that the Chamber want to hear about, rather than what other people either said to you or, alternatively, what you've read in statements or, indeed, elsewhere. It's your knowledge of these matters that I'm asking about and, I suspect, the Chamber would like to hear about. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but my knowledge is nil. I heard charges leveled against me by Mr. Davidovic. The investigators have investigated it. Why don't you produce the documents for us to see who's right? I heard it for the first time from Mr. Davidovic, and I'm telling you it's not true. That's why investigators went to see every one of those persons and to take statements, according to Rule 92 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as according to procedure. It's not hearsay; it's first-hand evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, once you are in a position again that you can consult with counsel, of course you can discuss this with Mr. Josse whether there would still be any chance to introduce any additional 92 bis statements on the matter, so it's not excluded. But at this moment reference to such statements, as Mr. Josse explained to you, is not what he asks you about. And as a witness you should answer the questions. You're -- temporarily you're in a different situation. Of course, any further submissions of 92 bis statements, Mr. Josse, will be considered if it comes to that, and then we'll hear from the Prosecution whether there are any objections, whether there should be cross-examination, et cetera. But this is not a moment in which we could hear such matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, I've got quite a lot more to ask you about Mr. Davidovic, but we -- in many ways what I've just put to you was his central allegation; namely, he had seen a document which you had signed, authorising the removal of people. What I would like you to comment upon, if you can - and let's not beat about the bush - what do you estimate his motivation for lying in this way to be?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't lying. He had seen a document but a different kind of document; however, he was angry with the SDS and the leadership and he spoke about the wrong document. Let the Judges see the document and they will see that he was -- he was deluded, that he was confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Stop there. This is important. Tell the learned Judges which document you had signed which you say he was, in fact, alluding to.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not I who signed, but there is one document signed by an MP from Bijeljina, Milan Tesic, as the government's commissioner, whereby he is authorised to conduct exchange of prisoners. And there is a stamp of Milan Tesic. It says: Government of the Republika Srpska, et cetera, et cetera. And he confused the two. Since Tesic was an MP, he thought it comes -- it came from me. That's why he had said so resolutely that he had seen the document. I don't understand why we can't produce this document here so that everybody can see what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, let's -- that's a procedural matter. I would not -- you assume that it could not be shown. If Mr. Krajisnik is in possession of a document which he thinks Mr. Davidovic saw and he is misrepresenting, Mr. Josse, you know how to introduce such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you a leading question, let's see if there's any objection to it. So don't answer this until we hear from our learned friends. Did you attempt -- did you personally attempt to put that document, during the course of your cross-examination of Mr. Davidovic, to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear no objection, so, Mr. Krajisnik, I would answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. You can find the transcript when I wanted to find that document to ask him whether it was the document, and you can see that from the transcript of Mr. Davidovic's evidence. However, there was a procedural problem, and I couldn't show it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, if you would be in a position to guide me to the relevant page on the last portion of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I -- I will be able to do that at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We'll then give it a follow-up. Of course, then the -- I take it from your last answer that that document that -- that it's in your possession, Mr. Krajisnik; is that a correct understanding? Or at least in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the Defence team should have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll see what Mr. Josse will do or will not do with it. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time I wanted to produce a lot of other things as well, but there were procedural problems. I wanted to produce statements and everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, what do you say about Mr. Davidovic's motivation for saying that you had had this conversation with Dragoljub Micic which I previously asked you about and you said didn't take place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have met people who love me a lot, and I have met other people yet who have never met me either but who seem to harbour a pathological hatred against me. I don't know this Mr. Davidovic, but he seems to have a terrible disaffection for all the leaders of the SDS. When he was replaced, he could have gone to the federal SUP to complain, but I have nothing to do with that man and I can't understand for the life of me what he has against me. And when he says that he hasn't seen me do a single positive thing, all right. That's his opinion. As for Mr. Tesic, this MP from Bijeljina, that's an honourable man, and I don't believe that he could be lying when he says that he had never talked to him. I can't understand what his motivation could be, apart from the fact that he is ideologically opposed to the SDS. I wasn't, after all, even a leader of the SDS, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm next going to turn to his allegations against you and others in relation to what I will call the appropriation of money. At -- in his witness statement, P764, he alleged that you, your brother, Radovan Karadzic, Radovan Karadzic's brother, Sarga Karadzic, were involved in an import/export business dealing with Serbia and other countries, usually Greece and Macedonia, which controlled all of the goods being brought into the RS. Profits in these ventures were huge, mere monopoly on the import of these products. And summarising, he said that you and your brother issued licenses on the goods that were destined for both the Republika Srpska and the Federation, and he was aware of this by implication because businessmen frequently met in Bijeljina to complete the trade and exchange.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I don't see how I can answer such fabrications. I kindly request the Trial Chamber to request from the authorities in Republika Srpska, or maybe Bosnia and Herzegovina, to investigate whether there is any truth in this. I had nothing to do with it. My brother even less. Nobody had any cooperation with Greece or any foreign country, nor could I have given any orders or instructions. It can only be pure gossip that he overheard and believed, but there is not a grain of truth in any of this. I hope the Trial Chamber can bind the authorities in Republika Srpska to send the appropriate documents to prove what I am saying, or Bosnia and Herzegovina or whatever. I never approved any of these deals. I was never involved in any of these deals, never had any monopoly. When I have to listen to all these things, I'm embarrassed by the sheer fact that it is being said in public, although I know it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic also alleged that you and Radovan Karadzic directly profited from the looting in Bijeljina of homes owned by Muslims, that that was facilitated - and I'm summarising here - through the offices of Drago Vukic, the local secret policeman; Predrag Jezeric from the Bijeljina SUP; and that money was effectively channeled via Vojkan Djurkovic to you and Radovan Karadzic through your respective brothers. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this is made up. There is a certified statement by Mr. Vojkan Djurkovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you because Mr. Tieger is about to object. Mr. Krajisnik, I - and I hope the Trial Chamber - can understand your frustration. Please answer the question: Is what Mr. Davidovic is alleging against you, is it true? That's what this Chamber want to know.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Again, I've asked you once, I'll ask you again: What's his motivation for saying these things; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say, by the same token, that during the war there were ideological opponents of the former communist regime who passed off all sorts of fabrications that were later subjected to financial expertise of the Registry. There was a man, an investigator, who searched for my alleged villas, apartments, real estate, et cetera. All this is fabrication, and the only thing that can absolve this man was that he may have heard it from somebody who was really ill-intentioned and deliberately circulated misinformation. The only money transaction that I can remember is giving 5.000 Deutschmarks to a young man who needed a leg prosthesis. I am not a Defence witness of Mr. Karadzic, but I know about this contribution for a -- for an orthopaedic prosthesis because Mr. Karadzic was involved in it and there was a document about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Listen to my next question carefully. Would you have any reason to suppose that Vojkan Djurkovic would say to Mr. Davidovic - or, indeed, apparently used to say it publicly - that he was taking money to Pale to you and Mr. Krajisnik -- you and Mr. Karadzic, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe he was trying to hide behind the broad back of some authority, but I don't think that's the reason. I think that Mr. Davidovic was simply not telling the truth, because this man, Vojkan Djurkovic -- I can't say that he made a statement, but he denies, at any rate, that he had ever said anything like it to Mr. Davidovic. I have as much to do with all of that as anyone else in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He alleged in -- that after the period of the indictment, in 1994, that he learnt that a motor car had been confiscated, he said, by the Bijeljina SUP from his son, that that car was given to Jovan Tintor, and that lists of cars confiscated by the SUP was sent to you and Mr. Karadzic, who then gave the vehicles to whoever you wanted, mainly people close to you, presumably as some sort of gift, political or otherwise. Any truth in that allegation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: None, none at all. I can only repeat what I said before: This idea that I disposed of cars, or Mr. Karadzic, for that matter, that has no truth in it. The MUP had commodity reserves. But I had actually forgotten about this allegation. I remember all the rest he said, but I had forgotten about this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Other evidence has been heard by this Chamber of cars being confiscated by different groups in Bijeljina, Zvornik, in 1992, paramilitary groups perhaps, other groups. Did any of this get back to you in Pale? We've seen your reference to some concerns to Mr. Mladic about events of this sort in Vogosca. Can you help the Chamber on this topic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thing with Mr. Mladic concerned new vehicles produced by the German-Bosnian company TAS. Those were unregistered new vehicles stolen by various people, whereas this case concerns cars, passenger vehicles, intercepted by all sorts of groups, seized, re-registered, and resold. So those are two different types of crime. As for the testimony of witnesses we heard here, they spoke about this other -- the second type of offence, when licence plates on a car are changed. I don't know who did it during the war, but MUP intercepted such vehicles many times, excluded them from traffic, and did I don't know what. I had information that that was going on, but who did that, why, for what purpose, I don't know. Simply, policemen would stop a vehicle in the street, check the papers, and realise the car had been stolen. I knew about such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'm looking at the clock, but before we take a break perhaps I inform you that the procedural issue on whether or not to admit any documents or whether or not Mr. Krajisnik was allowed to put certain documents to the witness, that was on the 27th of June, and you'll find it -- well, on from page 15 thousand approximately 240. The Chamber at that moment inquired into when these documents were received by the Defence, which was already some two weeks before that date. That was on the 12th of June, 2005, where the witness left The Hague on the 13th of June and then returned to be further cross-examined on the 27th of June. The documents were then put in the hands of Ms. Loukas. And even an opportunity was given to Ms. Loukas to decide whether she would give it a try, to cross-examine the witness on those documents although not translated yet, although not under all circumstances we have disallowed questions on documents which were not translated. I then take it that these documents remained in the hands of Ms. Loukas at the time. That's now almost one year ago, and it would certainly need some explanation on how they could be introduced at this moment where no questions were put to the witness at that time, and then even without a translation at this moment. Also, if it would have been a very important matter, of course one wonders why the matter had not been raised earlier, since the -- it was perfectly clear at that time what the issue was and what Mr. Krajisnik wanted to do is to confront the witness with - at least that's how I understand it certainly now - with a document -- another document which the witness Mr. Davidovic may have had in mind when he testified about a document signed by Mr. Krajisnik. Some questions were put to the witness in relation to -- or at least with -- in the back of the mind, I take it, of Mr. Krajisnik. The other document, for example, it was again asked to him who had signed that document, where he, I think for the second time, answered it was Mr. Krajisnik who had signed that document. One of the reasons why Ms. Loukas I think refrained from further questions to the witness was that she -- I think that's what she expressed, that it was -- the document was not from within the indictment period. And the witness at that time was asked when he saw that document. He said in 1993 without any further details. Whether that was early 1993, that might have made a difference. But that's just for your information at this moment what the procedural issue was at the time and where you can find it. We'll adjourn until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not desperately anxious to enter the fray over this issue of this document. We have been unable to locate it here. It is conceivable that it is in our other office, which is in another part of The Hague. For my part, bearing in mind Your Honour's comments, I'm not seeking to adduce it. But, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- I am painfully aware that I am trying to represent Mr. Krajisnik's cause here, and he thinks this document is important. He perhaps needs some guidance as to what will happen if he brings it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first ask, if it's mainly for the purpose of easily retrieving the document, would the Prosecution oppose if Mr. Krajisnik would give a copy of the documents he had in mind again now to Mr. Josse if, perhaps, out of a thousand documents Mr. Josse is not able to find it at this moment the documents which were given to Ms. Loukas at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we would have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Obviously there may be a variety of other issues arising in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, but at least Mr. Josse is handicapped at this moment because he doesn't even have access to the document itself so he can't develop any thoughts about it. Mr. Krajisnik, if you would have copies of those documents and if you consider it important to provide them to counsel so that counsel can consider whatever he wants to do with it, in full awareness of all the procedural aspects related to it, the Chamber will allow you to give them to Mr. Josse. Mr. Josse, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're going to move on to another aspect of Mr. Davidovic's evidence, and that relates to the Vance-Owen Plan and his assertion that sometime in 1993, I think it was, he attended a meeting one evening on Mount Jahorina at the Hotel Bistrica and that he was involved in some sort of security function there and that he actually attended a meeting of the SDS Deputy Club, where you said you didn't want that plan to be accepted. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role, as described by Mr. Davidovic -- well, he came as a forerunner -- he became before a number of officials; the late Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Cosic, Mr. Miso Takic. So his role was to see what our thoughts were with respect to the Vance Plan. I do not exclude the possibility that he was at Pale and that he was there in the place where we meet, in this Deputies' Club. He might have just been -- I exclude the fact that he was in the hall. As a foreigner he wouldn't have been able to come into the hall, but I'm sure he could have found ways and means of hearing what was going on. You have listening devices and different things of that kind. Now, whether he was there or not, I really don't know, I can't say, but he could have been in the vicinity because it was a mobile state. Now, as far as the Vance-Owen Plan is concerned, I can say that I was against the adoption of the Vance-Owen Plan. So he's right on that score. And I can explain why I was opposed to the Vance-Owen Plan. But in the most democratic way, everything else was put through. So you can't blame me. I was just against the Vance-Owen Plan as an individual. But as to the Deputy Club, he's not right that I exerted any influence on the deputies themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you now about the stance you took in relation to that plan; that's a topic that can perhaps be dealt with at a different point in your evidence. He also - this is Mr. Davidovic - in the course of his witness statement attributed, in part, to your door his removal from some of his activities. He said that you and Mr. Karadzic were close to Mauzer, that you and Mr. Karadzic complained to Mauzer about Mr. Davidovic and wanted him removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, you can answer the question, please, Mr. Krajisnik. The question is: Any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never knew about any issue of that nature. And for purposes of illustration, you have a decision by the Bijeljina Assembly where he was replaced. You also have the records, the minutes, and you can see that this was not on the agenda. Now, I never knew about the Davidovic case, nor was I close to Mauzer at all. Quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He asserted in the same statement that, in fact, he, Davidovic, was discussed at an Assembly session in September of 1992. The issue of his removal was discussed there. Any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have looked through all the Assemblies -- Assembly meetings. Perhaps Mr. Micic might have mentioned him. You have the minutes, you can look for yourselves. I did not come across anything like that, and even if he had mentioned him, that would have referred to some local problem, it wouldn't be something that was discussed. But in the stenogram, no mention is made in the stenographic notes that anybody mentioned Mr. Davidovic at that Assembly meeting. I don't remember. We didn't discuss it. Perhaps he heard from somebody or somebody told him that this was discussed in the Assembly, but I don't remember that we discussed it, nor do we have it in any of the minutes, because I checked, I looked through them, to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Finally, perhaps I should ask you this: Were you aware of his activities in suppressing and rounding up the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean for Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that I received at the time was this: That the special MUP unit had resolved the problem, the MUP of Republika Srpska. No other information reached me. And from the papers later on, I saw that he took part. But at the time, I didn't know about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What does "later on" mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean here, when I came here, and when we discussed this in court. But before that I'd never heard of Davidovic having taken part anywhere. It wasn't something I noticed. It wasn't something that stuck in my mind or had any reason to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And let's be clear. I know your evidence began on this topic, but let's go back to it. Until you were arrested, were awe aware of Milorad Davidovic at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. And when his name was put forward as a witness, I just couldn't understand who this was about, because there's a man called Davidovic from Montenegro, so I thought maybe that would be the person. I didn't know what witness they meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just very quickly. Can I have the particular page reference to the suppressing and rounding up of White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's a general proposition that comes from Davidovic's evidence, which is supported by KRAJ 682.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My recollection was that there was discussion about Yellow Wasps, but I don't have a specific recollection about White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, I'm sure that's right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The two colours are close. The animals are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, that's my fault. Does that change your answer at all? It was the Yellow Wasps Mr. Davidovic was involved in, so to speak, in suppressing and rounding up, and that 682 dealt with, not the White Eagles. Does it change your answer at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood you to mean the Yellow Wasps when I answered, so that would be it. And let me just add that I just heard about Zuca, not the Yellow Wasps. It was only here that I mentioned -- I heard mentioned the term the Yellow Wasps. It was Zuca at the time who was the leader of all of these paramilitary formations, and he was the head of the yellow wasps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Zuca" meaning "yellow," interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, yes, you're quite right. My answer is the same, the same answer that I gave a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mr. Tieger. Could we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, I repeat my question to you, which is where you said the only money transaction that you could remember is about the 5.000 Deutschmarks for the young handicapped man. What did you mean by "only"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the war all sorts of humanitarian aid came in, and it was in the -- within the province of other people. A man from Australia brought 5.000 Deutschmark - I have no idea why - gave them to me, and I put them in the safe. And I still have receipts to prove how that money was spent. I was trying to say that that's the only money I received during the war, those 5.000 Deutschmark, speaking of money, and it was for humanitarian purposes. I know that man, he was a native of Pale. It wasn't only humanitarian aid; other people dealt with humanitarian aid and they were in charge of distributing it, but I never received any amount apart from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Major financial transactions, would they continue -- well, let's say, in 1992 or was the situation such that no major financial transactions would be done by you privately? I mean, when I'm talking about major, that's -- well, let's say above 10.000 euros or so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you an example, Your Honour. For instance, two men came from the United States, bringing maybe 20, 30.000 dollars as aid. It was filmed by television. They brought this aid officially, and this was a different thing. This man just came to see me, I put it in the safe. Other people came to give money, too, but minor amounts. People would put that in the safe because they would initially bring the money to somebody who turns out to be absent, and then the money would be put in the safe. I didn't receive any other humanitarian aid on behalf of Republika Srpska without forwarding it, let alone the amounts that this witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that Mr. Krajisnik said the Assembly safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Assembly safe. That's what you said, Mr. Krajisnik? When you were talking about the safe, it was the Assembly safe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, its treasury, and that's where the money was paid out from. A little girl had leukemia and needed prosthesis. I don't remember anymore, but I have an itemised receipt how the money was spent. It is still in safekeeping over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's of course -- or I specifically asked about private money, but you are referring to other transactions. Any private transactions of major importance during 1992? I mean buying or investing or -- I mean I'm talking about operations of a larger scale.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid all misunderstanding, Your Honour, I don't remember whether it was at the beginning of the war or later, I bought some land in Arandjelovac. That was a private transaction with my private funds. I don't remember anything else. But as for the subject of that discussion concerning import and business deals, absolutely out of the question. I had nothing to do with that and neither my brother or I were ever involved in that, apart from that land I bought. I bought part of it and didn't buy another part of it. It was paid for by my private money, if that's what was referred to. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you: Do you remember what amount was involved, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it was 20 or 30.000 or maybe 15.000 Deutschmark. It was very cheap land. Mr. Jovanovic found that transaction. Maybe it was in the beginning of April. I don't know when I made that purchase, but it was before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No transactions of a similar size in 1992; investing, buying, whatever, so outside of the daily household expenditures on cars, gasoline, food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never. I had no investments, nor did I receive any money, even on account of humanitarian aid, nor did I invest anything. I don't remember. I found some money from humanitarian aid towards the end of the war and I bought a weekend cottage for my parents, but in 1992, nothing, nothing, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krajisnik -- Mr. Krajisnik, you exactly guessed what I had in mind to say to you. I see that there's not even a need to remind you that you should speak to one about the testimony already given or still about to be given, so I'll not remind you about it because you know. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, same courtroom, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.53 p.m.,
